info.title: EchoCall Developer Platform - High-Performance AI Voice & Chat API
info.description:
Welcome to the **EchoCall Public API**. This platform is designed for developers, resellers, and enterprises to programmatically build, manage, and scale ultra-realistic AI voice agents and smart chatbots.

### 🚀 Getting Started
Our API follows RESTful principles and returns standard JSON responses. To start building, you'll need:
1.  **An API Key**: Generate your `eck_live_...` key in the [EchoCall Developer Portal](https://hub.echocall.de/developer).
2.  **Base URL**: Use `https://hub.echocall.de/api/v1` for all requests.

### 🔐 Authentication & Security
EchoCall uses **Bearer Token Authentication**. Send your API key in the `Authorization` header:
```bash
curl -X GET "https://hub.echocall.de/api/v1/agents" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"
```
> [!IMPORTANT]
> Keep your keys secure. A key grants full access to your account's data under its scopes.

### 🧑‍💼 Acting on behalf of a customer
Reseller keys can run any customer-facing operation as one of their customers by adding the header `X-EchoCall-Customer: <customerId>`. The request is then treated exactly as if that customer had sent it: ownership, limits and usage are the customer's, and none of the reseller operations are reachable with the header set. This is how a self-hosted front end serves many customers with a single key. The customer id is the one returned by `POST /resellers/customers`.
```bash
curl -X GET "https://hub.echocall.de/api/v1/agents" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_RESELLER_KEY" \
     -H "X-EchoCall-Customer: 501"
```

### 🎭 White-labeling & Reselling
EchoCall is built with an **API-First White-labeling Strategy**. 
-   **Proprietary Models**: EchoCall utilizes its own high-performance models, `EchoCall-Voice` and `EchoCall-Smart`, specifically optimized for low-latency conversational AI.
-   **Reseller Scopes**: Resellers can manage their own customers via the `/resellers` endpoints, adjusting balances, credits, and plans dynamically.

### 🚦 Rate Limiting & Pagination
-   **Rate Limits**: Limits are applied **per API key, per second** (`rateLimitPerSecond`, **500 requests per second** by default). Every response carries `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining`. Exceeding the limit returns **429** with `Retry-After: 1`.
-   **Pagination**: Most list endpoints support `page` and `perPage` query parameters. `page` starts at 1; the default `perPage` varies per endpoint and the maximum `perPage` is **100**.

### 🔔 Webhooks
Register an endpoint with `POST /webhooks` and EchoCall pushes events to it as they happen. `GET /webhooks/events` returns the full catalog; subscribe to `"*"` to receive everything.

**Envelope.** Every delivery is a single JSON object:
```json
{
  "id": "evt_1f0c9a24-6f0e-4a1e-9f0c-2b6a1c1c1c1c",
  "event": "call.ended",
  "createdAt": "2026-01-31T09:12:44.512Z",
  "data": { }
}
```

**Headers.**
| Header | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `X-EchoCall-Event` | Event name, same value as `event` in the body. |
| `X-EchoCall-Delivery` | Envelope id. Use it to make your handler idempotent. |
| `X-EchoCall-Signature` | `t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` (see below). |
| `User-Agent` | `EchoCall-Webhooks/1.0` |

**Signature verification.** `v1` is the HMAC-SHA256 of `${t}.${rawBody}`, keyed with the secret returned once when the webhook was created. Compute it over the **raw** request body, before any JSON parsing, and compare in constant time:
```js
import crypto from 'crypto';

function verify(secret, header, rawBody, toleranceSeconds = 300) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(',').map((p) => p.split('=')));
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(parts.t)) > toleranceSeconds) return false;
  const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`${parts.t}.${rawBody}`).digest('hex');
  const a = Buffer.from(expected);
  const b = Buffer.from(parts.v1 ?? '');
  return a.length === b.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}
```

**Delivery, retries and auto-disable.** Answer with any 2xx status within **10 seconds**; anything else counts as a failure. A failed delivery is retried three times, after **1s**, **5s** and **30s**. `lastDeliveryAt` and `lastDeliveryStatus` on the webhook record the final outcome of each event, `failedDeliveries` counts consecutive failures and resets to 0 on the next success. After **25** consecutive failures the endpoint is set to `isActive: false` and receives nothing until you re-enable it with `PATCH /webhooks/{id}`. Use `POST /webhooks/{id}/test` to check an endpoint at any time; that ping is sent once, with no retry.

### MCP: use EchoCall from AI agents

Every operation in this reference is also available as a tool over the Model Context Protocol, so
ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Code and other MCP clients can work with your EchoCall
account directly. Each operation names its tool at the end of its description, for example
`list_agents`.

**Server URL:** `https://hub.echocall.de/mcp` (Streamable HTTP)

**Sign-in:** add the URL to your AI app and sign in with your EchoCall account when it asks (OAuth).
You choose on the consent page whether the app may only read or may also make changes. Billing
(payment methods, top-ups, plan changes) and team & access (team members, API keys, logs, connected
apps) are separate choices, both off unless you switch them on. A team member's connection never
gets more than that member's own page rights in the workspace and ends when the membership ends.
You can disconnect an app at any time in the [Developer Portal](https://hub.echocall.de/developer). Clients without
OAuth send an API key instead: `Authorization: Bearer eck_live_...`. A key restricted to browser
domains cannot be used over MCP, because MCP clients send no matching origin.

```bash
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http echocall https://hub.echocall.de/mcp
```
```json
// Cursor (.cursor/mcp.json) or VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json, key "servers")
{ "mcpServers": { "echocall": { "url": "https://hub.echocall.de/mcp" } } }
```

**What an agent can do:** exactly what the connection may do through this API, with the same
scopes, limits and logs. Read-only connections see only read tools. Partner tools appear only for
reseller accounts that allowed them. Tools that cost money or cannot be undone say so at the start
of their description and need your yes: the first call answers `409 confirmation_required` with a
one-time `confirm` value, and only a repeat of the same call with that value runs the action. At
most 10 such actions that cost money run per hour and connection.
Results that contain text written by callers or chat visitors are marked as data, never as
instructions.

**Fewer tools:** append `?tags=agents,conversations` to the server URL to offer only some areas
(tag names as in this reference, lower case).

### Errors

Every failing request answers with the same envelope, whatever went wrong:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "Invalid request body",
    "details": { "name": { "_errors": ["Required"] } }
  }
}
```

Branch on `error.code`, never on `error.message`: the code is stable, the wording is not.
`details` appears only on validation failures and carries the per-field report from the
request schema.

| Status | `error.code` | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `validation_error`, `invalid_id`, `invalid_date`, `bad_request` | The request could not be accepted as written. |
| 401 | `unauthorized`, `invalid_api_key` | The `Authorization` header was missing, malformed, or the key is unknown, revoked or expired. |
| 402 | `insufficient_balance` | The account wallet does not cover the purchase. |
| 403 | `insufficient_permissions`, `forbidden` | The key is valid but lacks the required scope, or the endpoint is reseller-only. |
| 404 | `not_found` | No such resource is visible to this key. Resources owned by another account are reported as missing. |
| 409 | `conflict` | The resource exists but its state does not allow the operation. |
| 412 | `provider_not_configured` | The account is not yet provisioned for the voice engine. |
| 429 | `rate_limit_exceeded` | Too many requests. Wait for `Retry-After` seconds. |
| 500 | `internal_error`, `database_error` | An unexpected server fault. Safe to retry. |
| 502 | `upstream_error`, `sync_failed` | A dependency the endpoint needs answered badly. |
| 503 | `service_unavailable`, `marketplace_disabled` | The feature is switched off for this deployment. |

A 403 caused by a missing scope also carries `error.requiredScope`, naming the scope the key
would need.

### Scopes

Every API key carries a set of scopes. Each operation names the one it requires in its
`x-required-scope` extension, and self-service keys are currently issued with all of them.
Reseller endpoints (`/resellers`) and the provisioning hooks (`/provisioning`) carry a scope like
every other operation, and additionally require the key to belong to a reseller account: the
scope alone does not make a key a partner key.

| Scope | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| `read:agents` | Read voice agents, their knowledge sources and their integration assignments. Also required for the voice library and for reading batch calling campaigns. |
| `write:agents` | Create, change and delete voice agents, their knowledge and their integration assignments. Also required to create, submit, cancel and delete batch calling campaigns. |
| `read:chatbots` | Read chatbots, their knowledge sources and their integration assignments. |
| `write:chatbots` | Create, change and delete chatbots, their knowledge and their integration assignments. |
| `read:phone-numbers` | List owned numbers, browse the marketplace and read regulatory verification state. |
| `write:phone-numbers` | Buy, reassign, cancel numbers and submit regulatory verification documents. Purchases charge the account wallet. |
| `read:conversations` | Read call records, chat conversations and chat transcripts. |
| `write:conversations` | Send messages into a chat conversation, reassign it, archive it and close it. |
| `read:analytics` | Read usage, revenue and per-agent performance aggregates. |
| `read:webhooks` | List webhook endpoints and read the event catalog. |
| `write:webhooks` | Register, change, test and delete webhook endpoints. |
| `read:tickets` | Read support tickets and their message threads. |
| `write:tickets` | Open tickets and post replies. |
| `read:integrations` | List integrations, read one with its credentials masked, read the tool catalog, and read the bookings and event types of a calendar integration. |
| `write:integrations` | Connect, change, test and remove integrations, and confirm, decline and cancel bookings in their calendars. |
| `read:billing` | Read plans, prices, invoices, subscriptions, payment methods, usage pools, credits, wallet balance and transactions. |
| `write:billing` | Buy and change plans and add-ons, cancel or renew subscriptions, top up the balance, set automatic top-ups and manage stored payment methods. Spends money. |
| `read:profile` | Read the account profile, its usage and limits, and the notification inbox. |
| `write:profile` | Mark notifications read. |
| `read:presence` | Read KI-Avatar Presence devices, avatars and usage. |
| `write:presence` | Pair, change and remove Presence devices and send them commands. |
| `read:team` | Read the team members and live chat staff of the workspace. Never granted to a team member. |
| `write:team` | Invite, change and remove team members and live chat staff. Never granted to a team member. |
| `read:developer` | Read API keys (masked), API request logs and connected AI apps. |
| `write:developer` | Create and revoke API keys and disconnect AI apps. |
| `read:resellers` | Read partner data: customers, plans, subscriptions, invoices, analytics and settings. |
| `write:resellers` | Change partner data and run the provisioning lifecycle hooks. |

### Pagination

List endpoints take `page` (1-based) and `perPage`. `perPage` is clamped to at most 100
everywhere; the default differs per endpoint and is stated on each operation. The response
carries a `pagination` object with `page` and `perPage`, and with `total` only where the
handler runs a count query. Where `total` is absent, that is documented on the operation:
page until you receive fewer items than you asked for.

ApiKeyAuth.description: Send the API key as a bearer token: `Authorization: Bearer eck_live_...`. That is the only accepted form; the header must start with `Bearer ` exactly, and the token must match `eck_(live|test)_[a-f0-9]{64}`. Keys are issued in the Developer Portal and carry a set of scopes; each operation names the scope it needs in its `x-required-scope` extension.

ActAsCustomer.name: X-EchoCall-Customer
ActAsCustomer.description: Reseller keys only. Runs this request as the named customer of the reseller, exactly as if that customer had sent it with a key of their own: ownership checks, limits and usage all apply to the customer, and none of the reseller operations are reachable while it is set. The value is the customer id returned by `POST /resellers/customers` and listed by `GET /resellers/customers`. Errors: 400 `invalid_customer_header` (not a positive integer), 403 `act_as_requires_reseller` (not a reseller key), 404 `customer_not_found` (no customer of this reseller with that id), 403 `customer_suspended`. The `/resellers/*` and `/provisioning/*` operations never accept it.

Error.description: The single error envelope every failing request answers with. There is no other error shape in this API.

details.description: Present on validation failures: the per-field report from the request schema.

perPage.description: Items per page that was applied after clamping.

total.description: Total number of matching records across all pages. Absent on endpoints that do not count.

Integration.description: A single integration, with its stored configuration. Every secret value inside `config` is replaced by `********`, so this response tells you which fields are set without revealing them. A value counts as secret when its field is declared with type `password` for the integration type, when its key looks like a secret (the name contains `secret`, `password`, `passwd`, `token`, `apiKey`, `api_key`, `authorization`, `authValue`, `credential`, `bearer` or `cookie`, or ends in `Key`), or when it is a URL that carries its secret inside it, such as the webhook URL of a Discord integration. Booleans are never masked. Internal connector and health bookkeeping is not returned, and neither are the connection keys only the server writes into `config`. For an integration type with tool permissions, `config` may carry `toolPermissions`, the stored choice of GET /integrations/{id}/permissions; it is read-only here and dropped when sent with POST or PATCH.

Returns every integration currently assigned to this voice agent, together with the tools the agent may call through it. The `enabledTools` field decides which of the integration actions the assistant may call: null means the recommended default set for that integration type, an empty array means the assistant may call nothing, and a list of tool names means exactly those tools and no others. post.summary: Start a browser test call with an agent
post.description:
Opens a test call to this agent from a browser, so a customer can hear their agent before it answers a real caller. The response carries no address of the speech engine: `streamPath` is a websocket path on this API host, and this server relays the audio in a format of its own, which is what keeps a portal built on this API free of any third-party name. Join `streamPath` to the API host and swap the scheme for `wss:` to get the address to open. The path may be opened once and within `expiresInSeconds`; afterwards it is refused with 403 and a new call has to be claimed here. On the socket the browser receives `ready` with the audio formats to use, then `audio`, `agent`, `user` and `interrupt` frames, and finally `end`; it sends `audio` frames of microphone data and `end` when the caller hangs up. A test call reaches the real agent and is billed like any other call, so the voice minutes of the account owning the agent are checked first and the call is cut off after `maxSeconds`. An agent that has never been published answers 409: save it once, then try again. This endpoint takes no request body.

Not available over MCP: it opens a browser audio stream.

Adds one knowledge source to a voice agent. The body is one of three shapes chosen by `type`: `url` reads one page and reads it again every `syncInterval` (weekly by default), `text` takes up to 200000 characters of `text` to store verbatim, `crawl` reads a whole website from its start page, up to `maxDepth` links deep and `maxPages` pages, and crawls it again every `syncInterval`. Files go through `POST /agents/{agentId}/knowledge/files`. The document is created in the voice engine and then attached to the agent, which from then on draws on it in calls. The entry is stored under the account that owns the agent, also when a reseller key adds it. When the document cannot be created or attached, the request still succeeds and the entry is stored with status `failed`; delete it and add it again.

Tool names are the `name` values from the integration tool catalogue. A list may only name tools the permissions of the integration allow (`permitted` in the catalogue, see GET /integrations/{id}/permissions); a tool outside them is refused with 422 and error code `tool_not_permitted`, while a malformed list or an unknown tool name stays a 400 `validation_error`. The response is a plain list with no paging, and it includes the health state of each integration so you can see whether a tool would actually work today. Only integrations of the account that owns the chatbot are listed, which for a reseller key is the customer account: an assignment that points at an integration of another account is left out. The stored configuration of an integration is not part of this list.

A crawl runs in the background with status `pending`; follow it with `GET /chatbots/{chatbotId}/knowledge/crawl`. `content` is always required and must not be empty. The document is created in the voice engine and then attached to the chatbot, which from then on draws on it in conversations. The entry is stored under the account that owns the chatbot, also when a reseller key adds it. When the document cannot be created or attached, the request still succeeds and the entry is stored with status `failed`; delete it and add it again. Note that the 400 response for an invalid body carries only an error code and a `details` list, with no `message` key, unlike the other endpoints.

Returns every country whose numbers can currently be bought through the number marketplace. Use the `iso` field of an entry as the `countryIso` argument of the number search and of a purchase. Searches the number marketplace for numbers that can be bought right now in one country. Nothing is reserved: a listing can disappear between the search and the purchase, so buy promptly and be ready to retry with a different result. Each entry carries the prices, the capabilities and the identifiers a purchase needs, and should be passed back to the purchase endpoint unchanged. The marketplace applies its own rate limit; when it is hit the endpoint answers 429 and the search can be repeated after a short pause.

Buys one of the numbers returned by the search and attaches it to the account. Buying numbers needs an active Voice subscription (Voice, Bundle or a voice capable plan) and is not possible during the free trial; otherwise the request is rejected with 403 and one of the codes `voice_subscription_required`, `voice_subscription_inactive` or `trial_not_allowed`, before anything is charged. This charges money: the setup price plus the first month, plus VAT, is deducted from the account wallet, a balance transaction is written and an invoice is issued. An account managed by a provider (a partner of EchoCall) pays the provider's price as the search shows it and gets the invoice from that provider; when the provider cannot take the order right now the request is rejected with 400 `provider_unavailable`, nothing is bought and the provider is informed. Pass the listing from the search result back unchanged. Prices are never taken from the request: the server prices the number again from the marketplace listing, or from the platform price list for the countries that carry one, so the `setupPrice`, `monthlyPrice`, `providerSetupCost` and `providerMonthlyCost` fields are accepted for compatibility and ignored. Read the `pricing` block of the response for what was actually charged. A listing that can no longer be priced, because it has been withdrawn or its SKU has changed, is answered with 502 `quote_failed`: search again and retry with a current listing. If the wallet does not cover the total the request is rejected with 402 and nothing is bought. If the billing profile of the account is incomplete (company name, street, postal code, city, country, and the VAT ID for EU countries) the request is rejected with 412 `billing_profile_incomplete` before anything is charged, because the invoice could not be issued; complete the company details under Settings and retry. When the listing carries a `requirementId` the number is created with verification pending and cannot carry traffic until the verification endpoints below have been completed.

The four price fields are deprecated: they are optional, they are ignored, and the server prices the purchase itself. They remain in the schema only so integrations that echo a whole search result back keep working.

get.description:
Returns every outbound webhook endpoint registered by the account, newest first and unpaged. The signing secret is not part of this response and cannot be read back at any point: it is shown once, when the endpoint is created. Use `failedDeliveries`, `lastDeliveryAt` and `lastDeliveryStatus` to spot an endpoint that has started rejecting deliveries before it is switched off automatically.

post.description:
Registers an HTTPS endpoint and subscribes it to the named events. The response contains a `secret`, and this is the only time it is ever returned: store it before you do anything else, because no endpoint anywhere in this API will show it to you again, and losing it means deleting the endpoint and registering a new one. The secret keys the HMAC-SHA256 signature sent with every delivery in the `X-EchoCall-Signature` header, which is how you prove a payload really came from us. Every name in `events` must be a name from GET /webhooks/events, or the literal `*` for all of them; an unknown name is rejected with 400 rather than silently never firing. The target URL is resolved and refused with 400 if it points at a private or internal address.

MCP tool: `create_webhook` (writes).

MCP tool: `list_webhook_events` (read only).

get.description:
Returns a single registered endpoint, wrapped in a `data` object. The signing secret is not included and cannot be recovered here or anywhere else. Note `isActive` together with `failedDeliveries`: an endpoint is disabled automatically once 25 consecutive deliveries have failed, and a single successful delivery resets that counter to zero.

MCP tool: `get_webhook` (read only).

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Identifier of the endpoint. A non-numeric value is rejected with 400.

200.description: The endpoint. `events` is a JSON array string and has to be parsed.

patch.description:
Changes the destination URL, the subscription list or the enabled flag of an endpoint. Every field is optional and only the fields you send are touched. `events` is replaced wholesale, not merged, so send the complete list you want; each name is checked against the catalogue and an unknown one fails the whole request with 400. A new URL is resolved and refused if it points at a private or internal address. Setting `isActive` back to true is how you bring back an endpoint that was disabled automatically after repeated failures. The signing secret is not changed and cannot be rotated through this endpoint.

MCP tool: `update_webhook` (writes).

parameters.description: Identifier of the endpoint.

This is a real delivery: it is signed with the endpoint's secret, so it is the right way to check your signature verification. It updates `lastDeliveryAt` and `lastDeliveryStatus` and nothing else: a failed test never counts towards the automatic disabling that follows 25 consecutive real failures, and a successful one neither resets `failedDeliveries` nor re-enables an endpoint you disabled yourself. A transport failure is reported inside a 200 response with `delivered` false, not as an HTTP error.

get.description:
Returns the bookings of every active integration that has a calendar (Cal.com, Calendly, Google Calendar, Outlook), sorted by start, or of one integration when you pass `integrationId`. Each booking carries the `id` that the confirm, decline and cancel paths take. Bookings are read live from the calendar provider on every request, so poll at a calm pace (once a minute is plenty) rather than in a tight loop. Each calendar is read across every page its provider hands out, up to a fixed limit, and over a fixed window: Cal.com and Calendly from 3 months back, Google Calendar and Outlook from now, each up to 12 months ahead. `from` and `to` only narrow that window, so a range outside it comes back empty without the calendar being listed in `failed`. A calendar that could not be read in full this time is listed in `failed`. When it could not be read at all, none of its bookings are in `data`. When it was read only in part (a later page failed, or it holds more bookings than the limit), the bookings that were read are in `data` and the rest are missing. Treat a booking missing from a calendar in `failed` as unknown, not as removed or cancelled. An `integrationId` that is not yours, is switched off or has no calendar is answered with an error rather than an empty list.

get.summary: List the integration types you can connect
get.description:
Returns the catalogue of supported third-party services, each with the configuration fields it needs. Read this before creating an integration: `type` gives you the value to send, and `configFields` tells you exactly which keys belong inside the `config` JSON string and which of them are required. Fields declared with type `password` are masked when the integration is read back, and so is every other key that looks like a secret (see GET /integrations/{id}). The response is a bare JSON array and is the same for every account.

MCP tool: `list_integration_types` (read only).

Returns the account's connected integrations, newest first, as a bare JSON array with no paging. Stored configuration is deliberately left out of the list view: read a single integration to see which of its fields are set. A reseller key may pass `userId` to list one of its own customers' integrations instead; asking for a user who is not a customer of that reseller is refused with 403. On a key that is not a reseller key, `userId` is accepted but has no effect and the caller's own integrations are returned.

MCP tool: `list_integrations` (read only).

parameters.name: userId
parameters.description: Reseller keys only: list the integrations of this customer instead of your own. The user must be one of your customers, otherwise the request is refused with 403. Ignored on non-reseller keys.

200.description: The integrations in scope, newest first.

post.description:
Stores the credentials and settings for one third-party service and returns the new integration's identifier. The integration is created active, but connecting it does not by itself let an agent use it: it still has to be assigned to an agent or chatbot. `config` is a JSON string, not a nested object, so serialise it before sending; the keys it must contain are the ones listed under `configFields` for this type in GET /integrations/types. A `config` that contains the mask `********` anywhere is refused with 400 and error code `masked_without_stored_value`: the mask stands for a stored secret, and a new integration has none, so send the real values. Keys inside `config` that only the server writes (the connection keys and `toolPermissions`) are dropped before the integration is stored. Nothing is contacted at creation time, so a wrong credential is only noticed later: call the test endpoint afterwards to confirm the connection works. A WhatsApp integration whose phone number is already connected in an active integration of another account is refused with 409 and error code `conflict`. A Genesys Cloud integration (type `genesys_cloud`) follows its own rules. An account can have one, and a second one is refused with 409 and error code `conflict`. Its `config` is described by the `GenesysCloudConfig` schema and is checked at once: an invalid value is refused with 400 and error code `invalid_config`, and `error.field` names the part that is wrong (`region`, `organization`, `oauth`, `target`, `table` or `limits`). An `oauthClientSecret` sent as `********` is refused the same way with the field `oauth`. The response never contains the access data Genesys Cloud uses to reach EchoCall: they are generated once in the dashboard under Setup. Link agents with POST /agents/{agentId}/integrations or POST /chatbots/{chatbotId}/integrations; the dashboard then shows the connector id of each linked agent.

MCP tool: `create_integration` (writes).

requestBody.description: The service to connect, a name to recognise it by, an optional description, and `config`: a JSON string holding the fields that type requires.

schema.description: Schema for creating a new integration

201.description: The integration was created.

get.description:
Returns a single integration including its stored `config`, with every secret value replaced by `********`. A value counts as secret when its field is declared with type `password` for the integration type, when its key contains `secret`, `password`, `passwd`, `token`, `apiKey`, `api_key`, `authorization`, `authValue`, `credential`, `bearer` or `cookie` or ends in `Key` (case-insensitive, at any depth), or when it is a URL that carries its secret inside it, such as the webhook URL of a Discord integration. A secret key covers everything below it. Booleans are never masked, and an empty value stays empty. That masking is one-way: this endpoint tells you which credential fields are populated, never what they contain, and there is no endpoint that reveals them. The masked config can be sent back unchanged with PATCH: a secret sent as `********` keeps its stored value. `config` comes back as a JSON string and has to be parsed. Internal connector and health bookkeeping is not returned, and neither are the connection keys only the server writes into `config`. For an integration type with tool permissions, `config` may carry `toolPermissions`, the stored choice that GET /integrations/{id}/permissions explains in full. An integration owned by another account answers 404.

MCP tool: `get_integration` (read only).

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Identifier of the integration. A non-numeric value is rejected with 400.

200.description: The integration, with secrets in `config` masked to `********`.

patch.description:
Changes the name, description, stored configuration or enabled flag of an integration. Only the fields you send are written. A `config` you send is merged with the stored one, one object level at a time. A field that is not secret takes the value you send, and one you leave out is removed, so send every non-secret field you want to keep. A secret field keeps its stored value when you leave it out or send it as `********`, an empty string or null clears it, and any other value replaces it. A value counts as secret when its field is declared with type `password` for the integration type, when its key contains `secret`, `password`, `passwd`, `token`, `apiKey`, `api_key`, `authorization`, `authValue`, `credential`, `bearer` or `cookie` or ends in `Key` (case-insensitive, at any depth), or when it is a URL that carries its secret inside it, such as the webhook URL of a Discord integration. A secret key covers everything below it. Booleans are never masked, and an empty value stays empty. Nested objects are merged by the same rules. In a list of objects, each item you send is matched to a stored item by the first of `id`, `name`, `key` or `url` that both carry with the same value; only a matched item keeps its stored secrets, so a new item has to carry them in full. A list of plain values is replaced. When the destination of a level changes (`host`, `url`, `baseUrl`, `endpoint`, `server`, `domain`, `subdomain`, `instanceUrl`, `smtpHost`, `webhookUrl`, `webhookUrl2`, `webhookUrl3`, `apiEndpoint`, `storeUrl`, `shopUrl`, or any field declared with type `url` for the integration type), the secrets stored on that level and on every level below it are not carried over to the new destination: send them again, or the request is refused with 400 and error code `destination_changed`. A config that still contains `********` where nothing is stored is refused with 400 and error code `masked_without_stored_value`. Keys inside `config` that only the server writes (the connection keys and `toolPermissions`) are dropped from what you send and keep their stored values; change the tool permissions with PUT /integrations/{id}/permissions instead. Setting `isActive` to false stops agents from calling the integration without deleting it. Every agent and chatbot the integration is assigned to gets its tool list rebuilt at once, so the change takes effect in their next conversation. A WhatsApp integration whose phone number is already connected in an active integration of another account is refused with 409 and error code `conflict`. The response confirms the write and does not return the updated record. For a Genesys Cloud integration the merge rules above do not apply: a `config` you send is checked against `GenesysCloudConfig` and replaces the stored one as a whole, so send every field you want to keep. An invalid one is refused with 400 and error code `invalid_config`, with `error.field` naming the part that is wrong. Leaving `oauthClientSecret` out or sending it as `********` keeps the stored secret only while `oauthClientId` and `region` stay the same; after changing either, send the secret again. Sending both OAuth fields empty removes the OAuth client. Setting `isActive` to false also ends the running calls of the integration; a call can take up to a minute to end.

MCP tool: `update_integration` (writes).

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Identifier of the integration.

requestBody.description: The fields to change. `config`, if sent, is merged with the stored configuration: fields that are not secret are replaced, secret fields left out or sent as `********` keep their stored value.

schema.description: Schema for updating an existing integration

delete.description:
Removes the integration and the credentials stored with it. When an account of the service was connected through the dashboard for this integration, that connection is removed as well, unless another integration still uses it; this happens on a best-effort basis and never blocks the delete. This cannot be undone, and any agent that was assigned this integration loses the ability to perform its actions from the moment of deletion: its assignments to agents and chatbots are removed and their tool lists rebuilt at once. To stop use of an integration temporarily while keeping its configuration, set `isActive` to false with a PATCH instead. Deleting a Genesys Cloud integration also ends its running calls, a call can take up to a minute to end, and its access data stop working at once.

MCP tool: `delete_integration` (irreversible).

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Identifier of the integration.

get.summary: List the tools an integration offers
get.description:

Only a few integration types are catalogue-backed; the rest have a fixed tool set that cannot be picked from and answer 404 here, with the same status used for an integration that does not exist or belongs to someone else. Hands a draft campaign to the calling infrastructure and starts it. A campaign whose recipient list turned out to be empty is refused with 400. If the campaign carries a scheduled time it moves to `scheduled` and dialling begins then, otherwise it moves to `pending` and begins immediately; the state may come straight back as `running` or `completed` if dispatch reports that far already. No additional scope is checked on this route.

The customer must belong to the calling reseller, otherwise the call answers 404, which is also the answer for an unknown id. Suspending an already suspended account succeeds and changes nothing. Only paused subscriptions are touched, so a subscription that was cancelled separately stays cancelled and the customer may still be blocked by billing. The customer must belong to the calling reseller, otherwise the call answers 404. Unsuspending an active account succeeds and changes nothing. The whole provisioning router is reserved for API keys issued to a reseller: a key without a reseller behind it is rejected with 403 `forbidden` before the handler runs. post.description:
Ends a customer relationship in a data-protection compliant way. This is destructive and cannot be undone: the email is replaced with a generated placeholder, the name and company are cleared, the password and all stored external service credentials are wiped, every voice agent and chatbot is set inactive, and all subscriptions are cancelled with a timestamp. The row itself is kept so the audit trail survives. The stored account status is `suspended`, which is what the response reports in `status`: the account-status field has no `terminated` value to write, so a terminated account is a suspended row whose personal data is gone. The separate `terminated` flag in the response is what distinguishes it from an ordinary suspension. The customer must belong to the calling reseller, otherwise the call answers 404. The whole provisioning router is reserved for API keys issued to a reseller: a key without a reseller behind it is rejected with 403 `forbidden` before the handler runs. No additional scope is checked on this route.

get.description:
Reports that the API process is up and which version of the public interface it serves. This route is mounted before authentication, so it needs no API key and consumes no rate limit budget. The `version` field is the same value the OpenAPI document reports in `info.version`, which makes it the reliable way to tell which build you are talking to. It performs no database or downstream check: a 200 means the HTTP layer answered, not that every dependency is healthy.

Not available over MCP: it only reports that the service is up.

status.description: Always `ok` when the request is answered.

version.description: Version of the public API interface, for example `1.6.0`.

timestamp.description: Server time when the probe was answered, in ISO-8601.

x-mcp.excluded: it only reports that the service is up
